name: Proto-cuneiform economic recording
summary: Around 3200 to 3000 BCE administrators in Uruk-period Mesopotamia recorded goods and quantities on clay tablets with standard signs, one of the earliest known forms of writing.
description: A structured system of signs and quantities recorded economic transactions on clay in the Uruk cultural setting; later phonetic writing is a separate development.
tier_reason: External written records support later administration, textual transmission and mathematical record keeping across generations; no single tablet inherits this consequence.

impact.note: Sign-and-number records on clay, a new administrative ability short of full writing, served many Near Eastern societies, and cuneiform writing, law, mathematics and astronomy later stood on them.

why: Large temple and city households in Uruk had to keep track of rations, goods and labour beyond what memory could hold.

date.label: Approximately 3200–3000 BCE
date.basis: Economic recording attests administrative practice in the named community, not later museum discovery.
